hints: Look at compound M, a trisubstituted cycloalkene, and recall what hot concentrated acidified KMnO4 does to a C=C bond when it breaks the ring open completely.
walkthrough:
See what reaction 1 really does**
You have 1-methylcyclopent-1-ene. With cold dilute $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ you would get a diol, but hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ is much more vigorous. It cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ bond completely and oxidises each end as far as possible.

Open the ring and assign the two ends**
Break the double bond in the five membered ring. The $\text{CH}$ end attached to the $\text{CH}_{2}$ chain becomes a carboxylic acid group, $\text{COOH}$. The $\text{C(CH}_{3})$ end, which has no H on the double bond carbon, becomes a ketone, $\text{COCH}_{3}$. Joining them through the remaining three $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups gives $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}$.
Final answer: N is $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}$ (5-oxohexanoic acid, a keto-acid with $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$).

hints: Compare the formulae of N, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$, and 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid, and think about which functional group NaBH4 reduces and how many [H] that needs.
walkthrough:
Spot what changes and what stays**
$\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is a selective reducing agent. It reduces ketones and aldehydes but it does not reduce carboxylic acids. So the ketone $\text{C=O}$ in N becomes a secondary alcohol $\text{CH(OH)}$ while the $\text{COOH}$ is untouched. That is a gain of two H atoms overall, so $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$ becomes $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{3}$.

Write it with [H]**
Using $[\text{H}]$ to show hydrogen from the reducing agent: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{3}$$

hints: Picture the shape around the ketone C=O carbon in N just before the nucleophile attacks.
Think about what happens when that flat carbonyl becomes a tetrahedral chiral centre with an OH group, and whether one or two stereoisomers can result.
walkthrough:
Start from the flat carbonyl**
The ketone carbon in N is $\text{sp}^{2}$ hybridised, trigonal planar. The nucleophilic hydride from $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ can approach the $\text{C=O}$ carbon from above the plane or from below the plane with equal chance. There is nothing to block one face.

See why two products appear**
Attack creates a new chiral centre at $\text{C5}$, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$. Attack from one side gives one enantiomer, attack from the other side gives the mirror image enantiomer. Both form equally, so you get a mixture of two optical isomers, a racemic mixture.

Final answer: The ketone C=O group in N is planar and can be attacked from either side with equal probability.
This forms two optical isomers / enantiomers in equal amounts (a racemic mixture).

hints: Use equation 1 as a model: a hydroxy-acid loses H2O between its own OH and COOH groups to close a ring containing COO.
walkthrough:
Close the ring intramolecularly**
5-hydroxyhexanoic acid has $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$. The $\text{OH}$ on C5 reacts with the $\text{COOH}$ on C1 in the same molecule, eliminating $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ just like in equation 1. Count the atoms in the new ring: five carbons plus one oxygen gives a six-membered cyclic ester with a $\text{CH}_{3}$ group on the carbon next to the single bonded O.

Final answer: P is the six-membered lactone from 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid, 6-methyl-tetrahydropyran-2-one: a six-membered ring containing $\text{-COO-}$ with a methyl substituent on the carbon attached to the ring oxygen.

hints: List the IR active bonds in N (ketone C=O, carboxyl C=O, O-H, C-O, C-H) and in the product (hydroxy O-H, carboxyl C=O, O-H, C-O, C-H).
Check Table 5.1 for where ketone carbonyl (1670-1740) and carboxyl carbonyl (1670-1740) absorb, and where O-H and C-O absorb, to see if they can be separated.
walkthrough:
Compare the functional groups side by side**
N has a ketone plus a carboxylic acid. The product has an alcohol plus a carboxylic acid. So both molecules contain $\text{C=O}$, $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{C-O}$ bonds. The only change is ketone to alcohol, but both types of $\text{C=O}$ fall in the same region.

Read the overlap from the table**
From Table 5.1, carbonyl / carboxyl $\text{C=O}$ is $1670-1740$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$, ester $\text{C=O}$ is $1710-1750$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$, so they overlap. $\text{O-H}$ (carboxyl $2500-3000$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$) is present in both, $\text{C-O}$ ($1040-1300$ $\text{cm}^{-1}$) is present in both, and $\text{C-H}$ is present in both. Because the bonds are in similar environments, the spectra look essentially the same and reaction 2 is hard to follow.

Final answer: Absorptions for N and 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid will overlap / be similar / indistinguishable.
Both molecules contain bonds in very similar environments, e.g. $\text{C=O}$, $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{C-O}$, whose ranges overlap so no distinct new peak appears.

hints: Recall that the M+1 peak is mainly due to 13C, about 1.1% per carbon atom, so use the ratio of the M+1 to M+ abundances to count carbons.
With Mr = 72 from the M+ peak and the carbon count, work out how many H and O atoms must be present for a cyclic ester containing only C, H and O.
walkthrough:
Count carbons from M+1**
Each carbon contributes about $1.1$% to the $\text{M}+1$ peak. So: $$\text{number of C} = \frac{\text{abundance of M+1}}{\text{abundance of M}} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = \frac{3.15}{95.5} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 3.0$$ So Q contains $3$ carbon atoms.

Deduce the lactone structure**
$\text{M}+$ is $72$, so $M_{r} = 72$. Three carbons account for $36$, leaving $72 - 36 = 36$. As a lactone it must contain two O atoms ($32$), leaving $4$ for H. That gives $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{2}$. The only cyclic ester fitting this is the four-membered lactone oxetan-2-one, a $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COO}$ ring.

Final answer: number of C atoms $= \frac{3.15}{95.5} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 3$
Q is the four-membered lactone $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{2}$ (oxetan-2-one), a four-membered ring containing $\text{-COO-}$.
